Trying to Conceive

Understanding ovarian cancer: types, symptoms, diagnosis and treatment

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Ovarian cancer is an umbrella term for several diseases with different origins and behaviour. Some cancers grouped with it start in the fallopian tube or the lining of the abdomen. Understanding the exact type, how far it has spread and the purpose of each test helps make conversations about treatment clearer.

What the ovaries do and how cancer develops

The ovaries are small reproductive organs on either side of the uterus. They contain the cells from which eggs develop and produce hormones, including estrogen and progesterone. Their supporting tissues and different cell populations can give rise to different kinds of tumours.

Normally, cell growth and replacement are controlled. Cancer develops when changes allow cells to keep multiplying in an abnormal way. A growing tumour can affect nearby organs, and malignant cells can invade tissue or spread elsewhere.

Spread may occur across the surfaces of the abdomen, through lymphatic channels or through the bloodstream. The word metastasis means that cancer has spread from its original site. A cancer that began in the bowel or breast and then involves an ovary remains classified according to where it started; it is not automatically a new primary ovarian cancer.

A mass in or near an ovary is not necessarily cancer. Benign tumours, functional cysts and other conditions can also produce a lump or an abnormal scan. The diagnosis depends on the clinical assessment and, when needed, examination of tissue.

Epithelial tumours and borderline tumours

Epithelial ovarian cancers are the most common group, accounting for about 85–90% of ovarian cancers according to the American Cancer Society. Their classification involves epithelial cells associated with the ovaries and fallopian tubes; many high-grade serous cancers are now understood to originate in the tube.

Not every epithelial tumour is malignant. Examples of benign tumours include serous cystadenomas, mucinous cystadenomas and most Brenner tumours. A benign tumour is different from an invasive carcinoma, even when both are described as ovarian growths.

Borderline epithelial tumours, sometimes called tumours of low malignant potential, form another category. They show abnormal growth but lack the destructive stromal invasion characteristic of invasive carcinoma. They need appropriate specialist assessment and follow-up; borderline is not simply another word for harmless.

Epithelial cancers also have distinct subtypes, including high-grade serous, low-grade serous, endometrioid, clear cell and mucinous cancer. Their behaviour and treatment can differ. Ask for the full pathology name rather than relying on the broad phrase ovarian cancer.

Germ-cell tumours

Germ-cell tumours arise from cells involved in the development of eggs. Some are benign, while others are malignant. These cancers are particularly relevant in adolescents and young adults, unlike the age pattern of many epithelial cancers.

Important malignant examples include dysgerminoma, immature teratoma and yolk sac tumour, also called an endodermal sinus tumour. An immature teratoma should not be confused with a mature teratoma or dermoid cyst, which is usually benign.

Many ovarian germ-cell cancers respond well to treatment. In selected cases, surgery can remove the affected ovary and tube while preserving the uterus and the other ovary. Whether chemotherapy is needed depends on the subtype, stage and other findings.

A favourable survival statistic is not a guarantee that fertility will be preserved. Cancer control, remaining ovarian function, treatment effects and individual circumstances all matter. Discuss fertility before treatment whenever possible, without delaying urgent cancer care.

Sex cord-stromal tumours

Sex cord-stromal tumours develop from ovarian tissues involved in support and hormone production. They are uncommon and include several separate diagnoses, rather than one disease with a single outlook.

Examples include granulosa cell tumours and Sertoli–Leydig cell tumours. Thecomas and fibromas belong to the wider group but are usually benign; they should not all be labelled ovarian cancers.

Some of these tumours produce hormones, which can lead to bleeding or other hormonal changes and may help bring them to medical attention. Many malignant stromal tumours are found while still relatively localized, but this does not mean every case is early-stage or needs the same treatment.

A granulosa cell tumour is its own tumour type. It should not be described as necessarily containing a mixture of granulosa cells, theca cells and fibroblasts. The pathologist’s classification guides the specialist plan and the follow-up required.

Related fallopian-tube and primary peritoneal cancers

The peritoneum is the thin lining covering the abdominal cavity and many of its organs. Primary peritoneal cancer starts in that lining. It is closely related to epithelial ovarian cancer and can have similar symptoms, microscopic features and treatment.

Fallopian-tube cancer can spread to an ovary or the peritoneum, and the original site may be difficult to determine when disease is widespread. This is one reason these cancers are often discussed together in clinical guidance.

Removing one ovary does not eliminate future ovarian cancer risk because the other ovary remains. Even surgery removing both ovaries and fallopian tubes does not remove every possibility of a related primary peritoneal cancer.

If surgery is being considered to reduce inherited risk, the decision needs specialist counselling about benefits, residual risk, fertility and menopause. Mention relevant ovarian, breast and other cancers in the family so the team can consider genetic assessment.

Stage and grade describe different things

Stage describes the extent of cancer in the body. Grade describes features of the cells and how abnormal they appear, interpreted within the particular tumour type. The words should not be used interchangeably, and stage IV is not a synonym for grade 4.

For ovarian epithelial and fallopian-tube cancer, stage I means disease is confined to one or both ovaries or tubes. Substages account for details such as surface involvement, rupture and cancer cells in abdominal fluid or washings.

Stage II involves extension within the pelvis. Stage III involves spread to the peritoneum outside the pelvis and/or specified regional lymph nodes. Stage IV involves distant spread, such as cancer cells in fluid around the lungs or disease within distant organs; spread on an organ’s surface is not always classified the same way as growth inside it.

Examination, imaging, surgery and pathology contribute to staging. Surgery can provide information that was not clear on a scan, but the team may begin with a clinical assessment when planning the safest treatment sequence. Ask which findings establish the stage and whether further results are pending.

Symptoms that deserve attention

Common symptom patterns include persistent or frequent abdominal swelling or bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, feeling full unusually quickly or finding it difficult to eat, and an urgent or more frequent need to urinate.

Other possible changes include indigestion or heartburn, constipation or diarrhoea, back pain, fatigue, pain during sex and changes in bleeding or periods. These symptoms have many possible causes. Their presence does not, by itself, establish ovarian cancer.

Seek assessment when symptoms are new, keep returning, persist or become more noticeable. You do not need to wait until they are severe, until every listed symptom appears, or until two weeks have passed if something is concerning.

Do not make unsuccessful self-treatment a condition for getting help. A change of diet, a laxative or extra rest cannot establish that persistent symptoms are harmless. If an initial explanation or treatment does not resolve the problem, return for review and explain what has continued or changed.

A brief record of symptom timing, eating difficulties, bowel or urinary changes and unusual bleeding can help the conversation. It is information for assessment, not a score for diagnosing yourself.

Why diagnosis can be difficult

The ovaries lie deep in the pelvis. Small changes may not be obvious on examination, and early symptoms can resemble more common digestive or urinary problems. A routine pelvic examination cannot reliably rule out ovarian cancer.

As a tumour grows or fluid accumulates in the abdomen, pressure on the bladder, bowel and other tissues may make symptoms more apparent. However, the idea that the disease is always completely silent until an advanced stage is misleading.

Many cases are diagnosed after spread has occurred. Earlier diagnosis can improve the range of treatment options and outlook, but a person with an advanced diagnosis should not be blamed for failing to recognize vague symptoms.

A normal cervical screening result does not provide reassurance about the ovaries. A Pap test examines cervical cells; it is not an ovarian-cancer screening test.

Screening is different from investigating symptoms

Screening looks for disease in people without symptoms. Diagnostic assessment investigates symptoms or an abnormal finding. The same test can have a useful diagnostic role without being suitable for routine population screening.

For people at average risk without symptoms, routine CA-125 testing and transvaginal ultrasound have not been shown to reduce ovarian-cancer deaths. False-positive results can lead to anxiety, further tests and unnecessary surgery. Research into better early detection continues, but an effective general screening programme should not be assumed to exist.

There is no universal requirement for annual vaginal examination from age 18 or annual rectovaginal examination from age 35 as ovarian-cancer screening. An examination should have a clinical purpose, be explained and take place with consent.

People with a strong family history or an inherited risk-associated gene change need an individualized specialist plan. Surveillance may be discussed in particular circumstances, but it should not be presented as a proven replacement for recommended risk-reducing care.

What the main tests can show

Assessment starts with a history and examination as appropriate. An abdominal or pelvic examination may identify a mass, fluid, tenderness or another explanation. A rectovaginal examination is sometimes relevant, but it is not mandatory for everyone. You can ask why an examination is proposed and ask for it to stop.

Ultrasound examines the ovaries and nearby structures. A transvaginal scan uses a probe placed in the vagina; an abdominal scan is another approach. The choice depends on the clinical question and individual circumstances. A scan can characterize a mass but cannot always determine its exact nature.

CA-125 is a blood marker that can be associated with ovarian cancer, but it is not specific to cancer. Benign conditions can raise it, and some ovarian cancers do not produce an elevated result. A normal result does not exclude every cancer, while an elevated result does not confirm one.

A specialist may arrange CT or other imaging to assess the distribution of disease and plan treatment. Further investigation can include laparoscopy, an image-guided sample or an operation, depending on the findings and proposed treatment sequence.

A pathologist examines tissue to establish the diagnosis and subtype. The team should select the safest and most useful way to obtain it; not every suspicious ovarian mass should follow the same scan-then-needle-biopsy sequence. If cancer is suspected, involvement of a gynecologic oncology team before definitive surgery is important.

Understanding risk and survival figures

Statistics need a date, a population and a clearly defined outcome. The American Cancer Society’s 2026 US estimates describe a lifetime ovarian-cancer risk of about 1 in 91. That is a population average, not the risk for every person, particularly someone with an inherited predisposition.

US SEER data for diagnoses in 2016–2022 report five-year relative survival of 91.9% for localized ovarian cancer, 70.1% for regional disease and 31.5% for distant disease. About 22% of cases were localized at diagnosis. These are broad registry categories, not a direct conversion into FIGO stages I, II, III and IV.

Relative survival compares survival in people with the cancer with that expected in a comparable general population. It does not mean a person has only five years to live, and a five-year statistic is not identical to a cure rate.

The subtype, stage, age, general health, treatment response and other findings affect the individual outlook. Older figures combining stages III and IV into a single percentage cannot describe every current diagnosis. Ask the treating team which information is most relevant to your own case.

The goals of initial surgery

Surgery often has several purposes: obtaining tissue, determining disease extent and removing cancer. A gynecologic oncologist can plan these aims together, taking account of the person’s health and the likelihood of removing visible disease safely.

For many epithelial cancers, the operation may remove both ovaries and tubes, the uterus and other affected tissue. Removal of an ovary and tube is called salpingo-oophorectomy; removal of the uterus is a hysterectomy. The exact operation is not identical for every tumour type or stage.

An open abdominal operation, or laparotomy, often uses a vertical incision to allow access to disease throughout the abdomen. A laparoscopic approach uses smaller incisions and a camera and may be suitable for selected assessment or treatment situations. Smaller incisions are not automatically the right approach to every cancer.

Debulking, also called cytoreduction, means removing as much cancer as possible. When feasible and safe, the aim is to leave no visible residual disease. Sometimes this requires surgery involving other organs, which needs discussion beforehand as far as the situation allows.

Pathology and surgical findings help guide further treatment. Before the operation, ask what might be removed, whether a more extensive procedure could become necessary, what recovery may involve and how fertility or hormone production could be affected.

Chemotherapy before surgery and the meaning of a second look

Some people have surgery first, followed by chemotherapy. Others begin with chemotherapy when immediate extensive surgery is unlikely to achieve an appropriate result or would carry excessive risk. Surgery after the initial chemotherapy is called interval cytoreductive surgery.

This is different from a second-look operation performed after completion of treatment simply to search for hidden remaining disease. Routine second-look surgery is not standard follow-up for epithelial ovarian cancer because finding disease earlier this way has not demonstrated improved outcomes.

Other tumour types or particular residual findings can raise different surgical questions. For example, selected germ-cell tumour situations may need further assessment or surgery. The reason should be explicit rather than assuming that every patient requires a first, second and third operation.

Follow-up may involve symptoms, examination, imaging and blood markers when appropriate. Ask what each follow-up test is intended to answer and whether a result would change treatment.

Surgery when cancer returns or causes an obstruction

Cancer that returns after treatment is called recurrent cancer. Further surgery may be considered for selected people, depending on where disease is found, previous treatment, the time since treatment and the chance of removing it usefully and safely.

An operation may aim to reduce tumour burden or relieve a particular problem. Disease can sometimes obstruct the bowel or the ureters, the tubes carrying urine from the kidneys to the bladder. Management may involve surgery or other procedures, chosen according to the situation.

Surgery for recurrence is not automatically beneficial for everyone and is not a guaranteed way to make chemotherapy work. Ask whether the proposed goal is cancer control, symptom relief or both, and what alternatives are available.

Persistent vomiting, marked abdominal swelling with inability to pass stool or gas, severe pain or a major reduction in urine needs prompt medical assessment rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

Other treatments and planning fertility care

Chemotherapy is commonly used, although the medicines and schedule differ across epithelial, germ-cell and stromal cancers. Targeted therapies may be appropriate for particular cancers, including some advanced or recurrent disease. Relevant molecular or inherited-gene testing can help the team discuss options.

Treatment should be planned around the exact diagnosis, general health and the person’s preferences. Ask about the aim of treatment, the expected sequence, how response will be assessed and whether a clinical trial is suitable.

If future pregnancy matters to you, raise this early. Preserving the uterus and one ovary can be possible in selected cases, but it is not safe or feasible for every cancer. The team can explain whether referral to a fertility specialist is appropriate and what can be considered without an unsafe delay.

Removing both ovaries before natural menopause causes surgical menopause. Chemotherapy can also affect ovarian function. Fertility, hormone symptoms and sexual wellbeing deserve discussion whether or not pregnancy is an immediate plan.

Physical side effects and when to call the team

Cancer medicines can affect healthy tissues as well as cancer cells. Side effects depend on the treatment and individual response; a list of possibilities does not mean that every person will experience them.

Digestive effects can include nausea, vomiting, constipation or diarrhoea. Mouth and throat soreness may make eating or drinking difficult. Tell the team early so that supportive medicines, nutrition advice or other adjustments can be considered.

Fatigue may have several causes, including anaemia. Low white-blood-cell counts can raise infection risk. Ask for clear written instructions about fever or sudden illness and whom to contact at any time; during treatment, do not wait for a routine appointment when the team’s urgent-call criteria are met.

Some medicines cause muscle discomfort, pain, tingling or numbness from nerve effects. Skin irritation or rashes can also occur. Reporting symptoms promptly helps the team assess whether supportive care or treatment changes are needed.

Many effects improve after treatment, but some can persist. Do not assume that every problem is unavoidable or that all effects will disappear immediately. Keep the treatment team informed about symptoms that affect walking, sleep, eating or daily activities.

Emotional and sexual wellbeing during care

Anxiety, low mood and uncertainty can accompany diagnosis and treatment. Emotional support is part of care, not an optional reward for coping well. A specialist nurse, counsellor, support group or trusted person may help with information and practical needs.

Treatment can affect sexual comfort, desire, body image and relationships. Fertility loss or early menopause can bring additional distress. Ask about appropriate help rather than assuming these subjects are outside cancer care.

Supportive medicines can relieve many physical side effects, but practical support also matters: transport, help at home, time away from work and assistance keeping track of appointments. Discuss the needs that are most pressing for you.

At appointments, ask for unfamiliar terms to be explained and request a written plan when useful. Understanding the diagnosis and the next step can make the process more manageable, even when some answers depend on further tests.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS guidance recommends assessment of persistent or recurring symptoms and returning for review if symptoms continue despite an initial explanation. Cancer tests have different roles, and a blood marker alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

The National Cancer Institute distinguishes screening from diagnosis and reports no mortality benefit from established general-population screening approaches. Its treatment guidance also distinguishes epithelial cancer from germ-cell disease, including different surgical decisions.

How BeMama can help

BeMama provides general education to help you prepare questions about the diagnosis, treatment choices, fertility and daily support. It cannot interpret a scan or recommend a cancer regimen. Bring the exact pathology name and your main questions to the specialist appointment.

When to seek help

Seek assessment for new persistent abdominal, pelvic, eating or urinary changes. Severe pain, persistent vomiting, marked swelling with inability to pass stool or gas, or a major reduction in urine needs prompt care. During treatment, follow the cancer team’s urgent instructions for fever or sudden illness.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ovarian cancer includes distinct epithelial, germ-cell and sex cord-stromal diseases; the full diagnosis matters.
  • Stage describes spread and grade describes cell features. They are not interchangeable.
  • Persistent symptoms need assessment; a normal Pap test does not rule out ovarian cancer.
  • Routine CA-125 or ultrasound screening has not shown a mortality benefit for asymptomatic people at average risk.
  • Surgery, chemotherapy and other treatments follow an individual plan; fertility and side-effect support should be discussed early.

Frequently asked questions

Does every ovarian cyst mean cancer?

No. Many cysts and tumours are benign. Clinical assessment, imaging and sometimes tissue examination are used to determine what a particular finding represents.

Does a normal Pap test rule out ovarian cancer?

No. A Pap test examines the cervix. It is not a test for ovarian cancer.

Can a CA-125 result diagnose ovarian cancer by itself?

No. It can rise for noncancerous reasons, and some ovarian cancers do not cause an elevated result. The result has to be interpreted with the clinical findings and other tests.

Are stage and grade the same thing?

No. Stage describes where cancer is present; grade describes particular microscopic features of the tumour. Both need to be explained in the context of the cancer type.

Does removing one ovary remove all future risk?

No. The other ovary remains, and even removal of both ovaries and tubes does not remove every risk of a related primary peritoneal cancer.

Will everyone need a second-look operation?

No. Routine second-look surgery after completed treatment is not standard care for epithelial ovarian cancer. Interval surgery after initial chemotherapy and surgery for selected recurrent or other tumours are different decisions.

Can fertility always be preserved?

No. It may be possible in selected cases, but depends on the diagnosis and treatment needed. Discuss options before treatment whenever feasible.

Do five-year survival figures tell me how long I will live?

No. They describe outcomes in groups over a defined period. They are not personal deadlines, and the treating team can explain which factors affect your outlook.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
